clinicalPearls: Defined by autoimmune Addison disease occurring with autoimmune thyroid disease (Schmidt syndrome) and/or type 1 diabetes (Carpenter syndrome); it is the commonest of the autoimmune polyglandular syndromes.
Unlike the monogenic type 1 syndrome, APS-2 is polygenic with strong HLA (DR3/DR4) association, presents typically in adulthood and shows female predominance.

Adrenal insufficiency is the pivotal and most dangerous component — insidious fatigue, hyperpigmentation, salt craving and postural dizziness may be attributed to other diagnoses until an adrenal crisis intervenes.

Starting thyroxine in an unrecognised hypoadrenal patient can precipitate adrenal crisis by accelerating cortisol clearance — always exclude or treat adrenal insufficiency before treating hypothyroidism.
A falling insulin requirement or recurrent hypoglycaemia in a person with type 1 diabetes should prompt evaluation for new adrenal insufficiency.
Component diseases emerge asynchronously over years, so a lifelong index of suspicion and periodic biochemical and autoantibody screening are needed.
Associated non-endocrine autoimmunity is common — coeliac disease, pernicious anaemia, vitiligo, alopecia and primary ovarian insufficiency.
First-degree relatives share increased risk, making family counselling and targeted screening worthwhile.
reference.pathophysiology: Autoimmune polyglandular syndrome type 2 is a polygenic organ-specific autoimmune disorder in which loss of immune self-tolerance leads to lymphocytic destruction of multiple endocrine glands. Susceptibility is dominated by high-risk HLA class II haplotypes (notably DR3-DQ2 and DR4-DQ8) with contributions from CTLA4, PTPN22 and other immunoregulatory genes, in contrast to the AIRE-mutation-driven monogenic type 1 syndrome. Autoreactive T cells and organ-specific autoantibodies mediate the injury: 21-hydroxylase antibodies mark autoimmune adrenalitis with progressive destruction of the adrenal cortex and glucocorticoid then mineralocorticoid failure; thyroid peroxidase and thyroglobulin antibodies drive Hashimoto thyroiditis or, with TSH-receptor antibodies, Graves disease; and glutamic acid decarboxylase, IA-2 and zinc-transporter-8 antibodies accompany autoimmune beta-cell destruction in type 1 diabetes. The glands are affected sequentially rather than simultaneously, reflecting shared genetic predisposition acting on different target tissues over time. Coexisting antibodies against gastric parietal cells, tissue transglutaminase and gonadal tissue explain the associated pernicious anaemia, coeliac disease and premature ovarian insufficiency. The clinical danger arises from the interplay of deficiencies, particularly the way thyroid hormone replacement unmasks latent cortisol deficiency.
additionalDifferentials: Autoimmune polyglandular syndrome type 1 (APECED) with mucocutaneous candidiasis and hypoparathyroidism
Isolated autoimmune Addison disease without other gland involvement
IPEX syndrome and other monogenic immune dysregulation disorders in the young
Secondary (pituitary) adrenal and thyroid failure from hypophysitis or panhypopituitarism
Infective adrenalitis such as tuberculous or fungal adrenal destruction
Thymoma-associated and drug-induced (immune checkpoint inhibitor) multi-endocrine autoimmunity
Wolfram syndrome and mitochondrial disorders causing combined endocrinopathy
additionalInvestigations: Short synacthen (ACTH stimulation) test with paired ACTH and renin for adrenal reserve
21-hydroxylase autoantibodies as a marker of autoimmune adrenalitis
Thyroid function with thyroid peroxidase, thyroglobulin and TSH-receptor antibodies
Glucose, HbA1c and islet autoantibodies (GAD, IA-2, ZnT8) for diabetes surveillance
Tissue transglutaminase antibodies and vitamin B12 with parietal cell antibodies for associated conditions
Serum electrolytes to detect the hyponatraemia and hyperkalaemia of mineralocorticoid deficiency
HLA typing and family screening where diagnostic clarification or risk stratification is needed
redFlags: Features of impending adrenal crisis — hypotension, vomiting, abdominal pain, confusion and profound weakness
Deteriorating glycaemic control or unexplained recurrent hypoglycaemia signalling new adrenal failure
Hyperpigmentation with weight loss and salt craving pointing to undiagnosed Addison disease
Clinical worsening after commencing thyroxine, suggesting precipitated hypoadrenalism
Severe electrolyte disturbance with cardiovascular instability
reference.prognosis: With early recognition and appropriate hormone replacement of each failing gland, life expectancy and quality of life are good, but the disorder is lifelong and further glands may fail over years. The principal preventable causes of death are unrecognised or undertreated adrenal crises, underscoring the need for patient education, steroid emergency plans and long-term surveillance.
pitfalls: Commencing levothyroxine before excluding or treating adrenal insufficiency and thereby triggering a crisis
Ascribing fatigue, weight loss and postural symptoms to the known endocrinopathy while missing new adrenal failure
Assuming diagnosis of one gland is the whole picture and not screening for the evolving components
Overlooking non-endocrine associations such as coeliac disease and pernicious anaemia
Failing to provide sick-day rules and emergency parenteral steroid provision to hypoadrenal patients

management: Lifelong glucocorticoid and mineralocorticoid replacement for autoimmune Addison disease, the pivotal and most dangerous component
Levothyroxine replacement for autoimmune hypothyroidism and insulin for associated type 1 diabetes, with antithyroid drugs, radioiodine or thyroidectomy for coexisting Graves disease
Exclude or treat adrenal insufficiency before initiating thyroxine to avoid precipitating adrenal crisis
Educate on sick-day glucocorticoid dosing, provide a steroid emergency card and injectable hydrocortisone for emergencies
Emergency management of adrenal crisis with parenteral hydrocortisone, intravenous fluids and correction of hyponatraemia and hyperkalaemia
Investigate a falling insulin requirement or recurrent hypoglycaemia in established diabetes as a possible marker of new adrenal insufficiency
Periodic biochemical and autoantibody screening for asynchronous new components, including coeliac disease and pernicious anaemia
Endocrinology-led care with counselling of relatives given the HLA-associated familial risk
